messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.reasoning:
The user says "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" but they provide sample mean, standard deviation, sample size, and population mean. They likely want the standard error or the standard deviation of the sampling distribution? The phrase "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" might refer to the standard error of the mean under H0: sigma/sqrt(n). But we don't know population sigma; we have sample std dev 1.4. So standard error = 1.4 / sqrt(40) ≈ 1.4/6.3249=0.2215. That is the standard error. Alternatively, maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic distribution: Under H0, the t-statistic has df=39, but its standard deviation is sqrt(df/(df-2))? Actually t-distribution has variance df/(df-2) for df>2. For df=39, variance=39/37≈1.0541, so SD≈1.0268. But more likely they want standard error.

Given typical context: "null hypothesis test" often refers to the test statistic's distribution. But the question: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." They give sample mean, sample std dev, sample size, population mean. They ask for standard deviation of the null hypothesis test. That could be the standard error of the mean difference: sqrt((s^2/n)+(sigma^2/N))? No, it's just sample standard deviation over sqrt(n). So answer: 0.2215.

We can also compute the t-statistic: (98.2-98.6)/(1.4/sqrt(40)) = -0.4/0.2215 = -1.805. But they didn't ask for t-statistic. They asked for standard deviation of the null hypothesis test. So I'd respond with standard error ~0.2215.

Thus I will output the standard error.
